place: A dry hillside camp at the edge of a grass meadow, in late summer after weeks without rain.
lines: make camp here
cook the rabbit over the fire
pack up and head to the ridge to watch the sunset
outcome: The player breaks camp without smothering the fire; the last logs are still glowing coals. A gust catches sparks and drops them into the dry grass a few paces off, which catches within minutes. By the time the player looks back from the ridge, a line of flame is spreading downwind through the meadow, and by nightfall it has burned a wide swath and only stops at a stream on the far side.

outcome: The player leaves the fresh meat hanging inside, close to where they sleep, instead of curing it or hanging it outside away from the hut. The meat itself starts to spoil in the warmth, and the player wakes to a chewed-open bag, missing meat, and claw marks on the door.

place: A small farming village with one shared well that every household draws from.

outcome: Under cover of night the player crushes poisonous berries into the village's only well and leaves unseen. The poison mixes through the water gradually rather than all at once, so the first households to draw water in the morning get the worst of it and several people fall seriously ill through the day; a few who drank less get away with cramps. By the second day someone connects the illness to the well, stops people drawing from it, and the village starts hauling water from the river instead until the well is drawn down and refilled.

outcome: The player partly cuts through one of the bridge's anchor ropes where the damage will not be noticed at a glance, meaning to strand or hurt whoever crosses next. The bridge tips hard to one side, spilling cargo and a mule into the gorge; the mule survives on a ledge partway down but has to be hauled out the next day, and the bridge itself is impassable until it is repaired.

outcome: The player holds an unlit torch underwater and tries to strike a flame onto it while it's submerged. Fire needs the wood to be dry enough to catch and needs air to burn in, and underwater there is neither: the torch is soaked through and any spark struck is smothered by the water before it can catch on anything. No amount of repeated striking changes this, because striking sparks does not remove the water or supply air; the player only wastes flint and steel and ends up with a torch too wet to light even after climbing out.
